chapters.title: Vafþrúðnismál

"Counsel me, Frigg, | for I long to fare,
In wisdom old | with the giant wise
Myself would I seek to match."⟦1⟧

en-thorpe.s: Odin:
Counsel thou me now, Frigg! as I long to go Vafthrûdnir to visit; great desire, I say, I have, in ancient lore with that all-wise Jötun to contend.

l: "Counsel me, Frigg, | for I long to travel,
in ancient wisdom | with the wise giant
I would seek to match myself."
"Heerfather here | at home would I keep,
Amid all the giants | an equal in might

en-thorpe.s: Frigg:
At home to bide Hærfather I would counsel, in the gods' dwellings; because no Jötun is, I believe, so mighty as is Vafthrûdnir.

l: "Heerfather I would keep | here at home,
among all the giants | I know of none
"Much have I fared, | much have I found,
Much have I got from the gods;
And fain would I know | how Vafthruthnir now

en-thorpe.s: Odin:
Much have I journeyed, much experienced, mighty ones many proved; but this I fain would know, how in Vafthrûdnir's halls it is.

l: "Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods;
and I would gladly know | how Vafthruthnir now
"Safe mayst thou go, | safe come again,
And safe be the way thou wendest!
Father of men, | let thy mind be keen
When speech with the giant thou seekest."

en-thorpe.s: Frigg:
In safety mayest thou go, in safety return; in safety on thy journeyings be; may thy wit avail thee, when thou, father of men! shalt hold converse with the Jötun.

l: "May you go safely, | come safely back,
and may the way you travel be safe!
Father of men, | let your mind be keen
when you seek to speak with the giant."
The wisdom then | of the giant wise
Forth did he fare to try;
He found the hall | of the father of Im,

en-thorpe.s: Then went Odin the lore to prove of that all-wise Jötun. To the hall he came which Im's father owned. Ygg went forthwith in.

l: The wisdom then | of the wise giant
he found the hall | of the father of Im,
and Ygg went in at once.

"Vafthruthnir, hail! | to thy hall am I come,
For thyself I fain would see;
And first would I ask | if wise thou art,
Or, giant, all wisdom hast won."

en-thorpe.s: Odin:
Hail to thee, Vafthrûdnir! to thy hall I am now come, thyself to see; for I fain would know, whether thou art a cunning and all-wise Jötun.

l: "Hail, Vafthruthnir! | I have come to your hall,
for I would gladly see you yourself;
and first I would ask | if you are wise,
or, giant, have won all wisdom."
"Who is the man | that speaks to me,
Forth from our dwelling | thou never shalt fare,
Unless wiser than I thou art."

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
What man is this, that in my habitation by word addresses me? Out thou goest not from our halls, if thou art not the wiser.

l: "Who is the man | who speaks to me,
Out of our dwelling | you shall never go,
unless you are wiser than I."
"Gagnrath they call me, | and thirsty I come
From a journey hard to thy hall;
Welcome I look for, | for long have I fared,

en-thorpe.s: Odin:
Gagnrâd is my name, from my journey I am come thirsty to thy halls, needing hospitality,—for I long have journeyed—and kind reception from thee, Jötun!

l: "Gagnrath they call me, | and thirsty I come
from a hard journey to your hall;
I look for a welcome, | for I have travelled long,
Far þú í sess í sal!
Far þú í sess í sal!
"Why standest thou there | on the floor whilst thou speakest?
A seat shalt thou have in my hall;
Then soon shall we know | whose knowledge is more,
The guest's or the sage's gray."

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Why then, Gagnrâd! speakest thou from the floor? Take in the hall a seat; then shall be proved which knows most, the guest or the ancient talker.

l: "Why do you stand there | on the floor while you speak?
You shall have a seat in my hall;
then we shall soon know | whose knowledge is greater,
the guest's or the grey sage's."
"If a poor man reaches | the home of the rich,
Let him wisely speak or be still;
For to him who speaks | with the hard of heart

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
A poor man should, who to a rich man comes, speak usefully or hold his tongue: over-much talk brings him, I ween, no good, who visits an austere man.

l: "If a poor man reaches | the home of the rich,
let him speak wisely or be still;
for one who speaks | with the hard of heart
will always come to harm by chattering."
"Speak forth now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the steed | that each morn anew
The day for mankind doth draw?"

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Tell me, Gagnrâd! since on the floor thou wilt prove thy proficiency, how the horse is called that draws each day forth over human kind?

l: "Speak out now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
you wish to make your wisdom known:
what is the name of the horse | that each morning anew
"Skinfaxi is he, | the steed who for men
The best of horses | to heroes he seems,
And brightly his mane doth burn."⟦12⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Skinfaxi he is named, that the bright day draws forth over human kind. Of coursers he is best accounted among the Reid-goths. Ever sheds light that horse's mane.

l: "Skinfaxi is he, | the horse who for men
the best of horses | he seems to heroes,
"Speak forth now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the steed | that from East anew
Brings night for the noble gods?"⟦13⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Tell me now, Gagnrâd! since on the floor thou wilt prove thy proficiency, how that steed is called, which from the east draws night o'er the beneficent powers?

l: "Speak out now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
you wish to make your wisdom known:
what is the name of the horse | that from the East anew
brings night for the noble gods?"
"Hrimfaxi name they | the steed that anew
Brings night for the noble gods;
Each morning foam | from his bit there falls,
And thence come the dews in the dales."⟦14⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Hrîmfaxi he is called, that each night draws forth over the beneficent powers. He from his bit lets fall drops every morn, whence in the dales comes dew.

l: "Hrimfaxi they call | the horse that anew
brings night for the noble gods;
each morning foam | falls from his bit,
and from it comes the dew in the valleys."
"Speak forth now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the river | that 'twixt the realms
Of the gods and the giants goes?"

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Tell me, Gagnrâd! since on the floor thou wilt prove thy proficiency, how the stream is called, which earth divides between the Jötuns and the Gods?

l: "Speak out now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
you wish to make your wisdom known:
what is the name of the river | that between the realms
of the gods and the giants runs?"
"Ifing is the river | that 'twixt the realms
Of the gods and the giants goes;
For all time ever | open it flows,
No ice on the river there is."⟦16⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Ifing the stream is called which earth divides between the Jötuns and the Gods: open shall it run throughout all time. On that stream no ice shall be.

l: "Ifing is the river | that between the realms
of the gods and the giants runs;
for all time | it flows open,
there is no ice on the river."
"Speak forth now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
Thou wouldst thy wisdom make known:
What name has the field | where in fight shall meet

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Tell me, Gagnrâd! since on the floor thou wilt prove thy proficiency, how that plain is called, where in fight shall meet Surt and the gentle Gods?

l: "Speak out now, Gagnrath, | if there from the floor
you wish to make your wisdom known:
what is the name of the field | where they will meet in battle,
"Vigrith is the field | where in fight shall meet
A hundred miles | each way does it measure.
And so are its boundaries set."⟦18⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Vigrid the plain is called where in fight shall meet Surt and the gentle Gods; a hundred rasts it is on every side. That plain is to them decreed.

l: "Vigrith is the field | where they will meet in battle,
a hundred miles | it measures each way,
and so its boundaries are set."
"Wise art thou, guest! | To my bench shalt thou go,
In our seats let us speak together;
Here in the hall | our heads, O guest,
Shall we wager our wisdom upon."⟦19⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Wise art thou, O guest! Approach the Jötuns bench, and sitting let us together talk; we will our heads in the hall pledge, guest! for wise utterance.

l: "You are wise, guest! | Come to my bench,
let us speak together in our seats;
here in the hall, | guest, we shall wager
"First answer me well, | if thy wisdom avails,
And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
In earliest time | whence came the earth,
Or the sky, thou giant sage?"⟦20⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me first, if thy wit suffices, and thou, Vafthrûdnir! knowest, whence first came the earth, and the high heaven, thou, sagacious Jötun?

l: "First, answer me well, | if your wisdom serves,
and you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where in the earliest time | did the earth come from,
or the sky, you wise giant?"
"Out of Ymir's flesh | was fashioned the earth,
And the mountains were made of his bones;
The sky from the frost-cold | giant's skull,
And the ocean out of his blood."⟦21⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
From Ymir's flesh the earth was formed, and from his bones the hills, the heaven from the skull of that ice-cold giant, and from his blood the sea.

l: "Out of Ymir's flesh | the earth was fashioned,
and the mountains were made of his bones;
the sky from the frost-cold | giant's skull,
and the ocean out of his blood."
"Next answer me well, | if thy wisdom avails,
And thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence came the moon, | o'er the world of men
That fares, and the flaming sun?"⟦22⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me secondly, if thy wit suffices, and thou, Vafthrûdnir! knowest, whence came the moon, which over mankind passes, and the sun likewise?

l: "Next, answer me well, | if your wisdom serves,
and you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where did the moon come from, | that travels over the world of men,
"Mundilferi is he | who begat the moon,
The round of heaven | each day they run,
To tell the time for men."⟦23⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Mundilfœri hight he, who the moon's father is, and eke the sun's: round heaven journey each day they must, to count years for men.

l: "Mundilferi is he | who begot the moon,
the round of heaven | they run each day,
to tell the time for men."
"Third answer me well, | if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence came the day, | o'er mankind that fares,
Or night with the narrowing moon?"

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me thirdly, since thou art called wise, and if thou, Vafthrûdnir! knowest, whence came the day, which over people passes, and night with waning moons?

l: "Third, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where did the day come from, | that travels over mankind,
or night with the waning moon?"
"The father of day | is Delling called,
And the night was begotten by Nor;
Full moon and old | by the gods were fashioned,
To tell the time for men."⟦25⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Delling hight he who the day's father is, but night was of Nörvi born; the new and waning moons the beneficent powers created, to count years for men.

l: "The father of day | is called Delling,
and the night was begotten by Nor;
the full moon and the old | were fashioned by the gods,
to tell the time for men."
"Fourth answer me well, | if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence did winter come, | or the summer warm,

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me fourthly, since they pronounce thee sage, and if thou, Vafthrûdnir! knowest, whence winter came, and warm summer first among the wise gods?

l: "Fourth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where did winter come from, | or the warm summer,
"Vindsval he was | who was winter's father,

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Vindsval hight he, who winter's father is, and Svâsud summer's; yearly they both shall ever journey, until the powers perish.

l: "Vindsval he was | who was winter's father,
"Fifth answer me well, | if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
What giant first | was fashioned of old,
And the eldest of Ymir's kin?"⟦28⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me fifthly, since they pronounce thee sage, and if thou, Vafthrûdnir! knowest, which of the Æsir earliest, or of Ymir's sons, in days of old existed?

l: "Fifth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
what giant was first | fashioned of old,
and the eldest of Ymir's kin?"
Thruthgelmir's son | was the giant strong,

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Countless winters, ere earth was formed, was Bergelmir born; Thrûdgelmir was his sire, his grandsire Aurgelmir.

l: "Countless winters | before the earth was made
Thruthgelmir's son | was the strong giant,
"Sixth answer me well, | if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence did Aurgelmir come | with the giants' kin,

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me sixthly, since thou art called wise, and if thou, Vafthrûdnir! knowest, whence first came Aurgelmir, among the Jötun's sons, thou sagacious Jötun?

l: "Sixth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where did Aurgelmir come from | with the giants' kin,
því er þat æ allt til atalt."
því er það æ allt til atalt."
And waxed till a giant it was;
And thence arose | our giants' race,
And thus so fierce are we found."⟦31⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
From Elivâgar sprang venom drops, which grew till they became a Jötun; but sparks flew from the south-world: to the ice the fire gave life.

l: and grew until it was a giant;
and from it arose | our race of giants,
and that is why we are found so fierce."
"Seventh answer me well, | if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
How begat he children, | the giant grim,

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me seventhly, since thou are called wise, and if thou knowest, Vafthrûdnir! how he children begat, the bold Jötun, as he had no giantess's company?

l: "Seventh, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
how did he beget children, | the grim giant,
"They say 'neath the arms | of the giant of ice
And foot with foot | did the wise one fashion
A son that six heads bore."⟦33⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Under the armpit grew, 'tis said, of the Hrîmthurs, a girl and boy together; foot with foot begat, of that wise Jötun, a six-headed son.

l: "They say that under the arms | of the giant of ice
a boy and a girl grew together;
and foot with foot | the wise one fashioned
a son who had six heads."
"Eighth answer me well, | if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
What farthest back | dost thou bear in mind?
For wide is thy wisdom, giant!"

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me eighthly, since thou art called wise, and if thou knowest, Vafthrûdnir! what thou doest first remember, or earliest knowest? Thou art an all-wise Jötun.

l: "Eighth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
what do you bear in mind | from farthest back?
For your wisdom is wide, giant!"
This first knew I well, | when the giant wise
In a boat of old was borne."⟦35⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Countless winters, ere earth was formed, Bergelmir was born. That I first remember, when that wise Jötun in an ark was laid.

l: "Countless winters | before the earth was made
the first thing I knew well | was when the wise giant
was carried long ago in a boat."
æ menn han sjalfan of sjá."
æ menn han sjálfan of sjá."
"Ninth answer me well, | if wise thou art called,
If thou knowest it, Vafthruthnir, now:
Whence comes the wind | that fares o'er the waves

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me ninthly, since thou art called wise, and if thou knowest, Vafthrûdnir! whence the wind comes, that over ocean passes, itself invisible to man?

l: "Ninth, answer me well, | if you are called wise,
if you know it, Vafthruthnir, now:
where does the wind come from | that travels over the waves
"In an eagle's guise | at the end of heaven
And from his wings | does the wind come forth
To move o'er the world of men."⟦37⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Hræsvelg he is called, who at the end of heaven sits, a Jötun in an eagle's plumage: from his wings comes, it is said, the wind, that over all men passes.

l: "In an eagle's shape | at the end of heaven
and from his wings | the wind comes forth
to move over the world of men."
"Tenth answer me now, | if thou knowest all
The fate that is fixed for the gods:
Whence came up Njorth | to the kin of the gods,—
(Rich in temples | and shrines he rules,—)
Though of gods he was never begot?"⟦38⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:

Tell me tenthly, since thou all the origin of the gods knowest, Vafthrûdnir! whence Niörd came among the Æsir's sons? O'er fanes and offer-steads he rules by hundreds, yet was not among the Æsir born.

l: "Tenth, answer me now, | if you know all
the fate that is fixed for the gods:
where did Njorth come from | to the kin of the gods,
(rich in temples | and shrines he rules,)
though he was never begotten of gods?"
"In the home of the Wanes | did the wise ones create him,
And gave him as pledge to the gods;
At the fall of the world | shall he fare once more
Home to the Wanes so wise."

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
In Vanaheim wise powers him created, and to the gods a hostage gave. At the world's dissolution, he will return to the wise Vanir.

l: "In the home of the Wanes | the wise ones created him,
and gave him as a pledge to the gods;
at the fall of the world | he will go once more
home to the Wanes so wise."
Each day to fight go forth?"⟦40⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me eleventhly, since all the condition of the gods thou knowest, Vafthrûdnir! what the Einheriar do in Hærfather's halls, until the powers perish?

l: go out each day to fight?"
Each day to fight go forth;
They fell each other, | and fare from the fight
All healed full soon to sit."⟦41⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
All the Einheriar in Odin's halls each day together fight; the fallen they choose, and from the conflict ride; beer with the Æsir drink, of Sæhrimnir eat their fill, then sit in harmony together.

l: go out each day to fight;
they cut each other down, | and come from the fight
"Twelfth answer me now | how all thou knowest
Of the fate that is fixed for the gods;
Of the runes of the gods | and the giants' race
The truth indeed dost thou tell,

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Tell me twelfthly, as thou all the condition of the gods knowest, Vafthrûdnir! of the Jötuns' secrets, and of all the gods', say what truest is, thou all-knowing Jötun!

l: "Twelfth, answer me now | how you know all
of the fate that is fixed for the gods;
of the runes of the gods | and the giants' race
you do indeed tell the truth,
"Of the runes of the gods | and the giants' race
The truth indeed can I tell,
(For to every world have I won;)
To nine worlds came I, | to Niflhel beneath,
The home where dead men dwell."⟦43⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Of the secrets of the Jötuns and of all the gods, I can truly tell; for I have over each world travelled; to nine worlds I came, to Niflhel beneath: here die men from Hel.

l: "Of the runes of the gods | and the giants' race
I can indeed tell the truth,
(for I have made my way to every world;)
to nine worlds I came, | to Niflhel beneath,
the home where dead men dwell."
"Much have I fared, | much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What shall live of mankind | when at last there comes

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Much have I journeyed, much experienced, mighty ones many proved. What mortals will live, when the great "Fimbul"-winter shall from men have passed?

l: "Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
what will live of mankind | when at last there comes
The morning dews | for meat shall they have,
Such food shall men then find."⟦45⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Lîf and Lîfthrasir; but they will be concealed in Hoddmimir's holt. The morning dews they will have for food. From them shall men be born.

l: "In Hoddmimir's wood | they will hide themselves,
the morning dews | they will have for food,
such food will men then find."
"Much have I fared, | much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
Whence comes the sun | to the smooth sky back,
When Fenrir has snatched it forth?"⟦46⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Much have I journeyed, much experienced, mighty ones many proved. Whence will come the sun in that fair heaven, when Fenrir has this devoured?

l: "Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
where does the sun come from | back to the smooth sky,
when Fenrir has snatched it away?"
Her mother's paths | shall the maiden tread
When the gods to death have gone."⟦47⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
A daughter shall Alfrödull bear, ere Fenrir shall have swallowed her. The maid shall ride, when the powers die, on her mother's course.

l: her mother's paths | the maiden will tread
when the gods have gone to death."
"Much have I fared, | much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What maidens are they, | so wise of mind.
That forth o'er the sea shall fare?"

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Much have I journeyed, etc. Who are the maidens that o'er the ocean travel, wise of spirit, journey?

l: "Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
what maidens are they, | so wise of mind,
who will travel out over the sea?"
"O'er Mogthrasir's hill | shall the maidens pass,
And three are their throngs that come;
They all shall protect | the dwellers on earth,
Though they come of the giants' kin."⟦49⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
O'er people's dwellings three descend of Mögthrasir's maidens, the sole Hamingiur who are in the world, although with Jötuns nurtured.

l: "Over Mogthrasir's hill | the maidens will pass,
and three are their throngs that come;
they will all protect | the dwellers on earth,
though they come of the giants' kin."
"Much have I fared, | much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
Who then shall rule | the realm of the gods,
When the fires of Surt have sunk?"⟦50⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Much have I journeyed, etc. Which of the Æsir will rule o'er the gods' possession, when Surt's fire shall be quenched?

l: "Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
who then will rule | the realm of the gods,
when the fires of Surt have sunk?"
"In the gods' home Vithar | and Vali shall dwell,
When the fires of Surt have sunk;
Mothi and Magni | shall Mjollnir have

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
Vidar and Vali will the gods' holy fanes inhabit, when Surt's fire shall be quenched. Môdi and Magni will Miöllnir possess, and warfare strive to end.

l: "In the gods' home Vithar | and Vali will live,
when the fires of Surt have sunk;
Mothi and Magni | will have Mjollnir
"Much have I fared, | much have I found,
Much have I got of the gods:
What shall bring the doom | of death to Othin,
When the gods to destruction go?"

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Much have I journeyed, etc. What of Odin will the life's end be, when the powers perish?

l: "Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
what will bring the doom | of death to Othin,
when the gods go to destruction?"
"The wolf shall fell | the father of men,
The terrible jaws | shall he tear apart,
And so the wolf shall he slay."⟦53⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:
The wolf will the father of men devour; him Vidar will avenge: he his cold jaws will cleave, in conflict with the wolf.

l: "The wolf will bring down | the father of men,
the terrible jaws | he will tear apart,
and so he will kill the wolf."
"Much have I fared, | much have I found,
Much have I got from the gods:
What spake Othin himself | in the ears of his son,
Ere in the bale-fire he burned?"⟦54⟧

en-thorpe.s: Gagnrâd:
Much have I journeyed, etc. What said Odin in his son's ear, ere he on the pile was laid?

l: "Much have I travelled, | much have I found,
much have I got from the gods:
what did Othin himself say | in the ears of his son,
before he burned on the funeral pyre?"
"No man can tell | what in olden time
Thou spak'st in the ears of thy son;
With fated mouth | the fall of the gods
And mine olden tales have I told;
With Othin in knowledge | now have I striven,
And ever the wiser thou art."⟦55⟧

en-thorpe.s: Vafthrûdnir:

That no one knoweth, what thou in days of old saidst in thy son's ear. With dying mouth my ancient saws I have said, and the gods' destruction. With Odin I have contended in wise utterances: of men thou ever art the wisest!

l: "No man can tell | what in days of old
you said in the ears of your son;
with a doomed mouth | I have told of the fall of the gods
with Othin in knowledge | I have now striven,
and you are always the wiser."

notes.s: The phrases "Othin spake," "Frigg spake," etc. appear in abbreviated form in both manuscripts. Frigg: Othin's wife; cf. Voluspo, 34 and note. Vafthruthnir ("the Mighty in Riddles"): nothing is known of this giant beyond what is told in this poem.
Heerfather ("Father of the Host"): Othin.
This single narrative stanza is presumably a later  interpolation. Im: the name appears to be corrupt, but we know nothing of any son of Vafthruthnir. Ygg ("the Terrible"): Othin.
Gagnrath ("the Gain-Counsellor"): Othin on his travels always assumes a name other than his own.
This stanza sounds very much like many of those in the first part of the Hovamol, and may have been introduced here from some such source.
Skinfaxi: "Shining-Mane."
Here, and in general throughout the poem, the two-line introductory formulæ are abbreviated in the manuscripts.
Hrimfaxi: "Frosty-Mane."
Ifing: there is no other reference to this river, which never freezes, so that the giants cannot cross it.
Surt: the ruler of the fire-world (Muspellsheim), who comes to attack the gods in the last battle; cf. Voluspo, 52.
Vigrith: "the Field of Battle." Snorri quotes this stanza. A hundred miles: a general phrase for a vast distance.
With this stanza Vafthruthnir, sufficiently impressed with his guest's wisdom to invite him to share his own seat, resigns the questioning to Othin.
The fragmentary version of this poem in the Arnamagnæan Codex begins in the middle of the first line of this stanza.
Ymir: the giant out of whose body the gods made the world; cf. Voluspo, 3 and note.
In this and in Othin's following questions, both manuscripts replace the words "next," "third," "fourth," etc., by Roman numerals.

Mundilferi ("the Turner"?): known only as the father of Mani (the Moon) and Sol (the Sun). Note that, curiously enough, Mani is the boy and Sol the girl. According to Snorri, Sol drove the horses of the sun, and Mani those of the moon, for the gods, indignant that they should have been given such imposing names, took them from their father to perform these tasks. Cf. Grimnismol, 37.

Delling ("the Dayspring"? Probably another form of the name, Dogling, meaning "Son of the Dew" is more correct): the husband of Not (Night); their son was Dag (Day); cf. Hovamol, 161. Nor: Snorri calls the father of Night Norvi or Narfi, and puts him among the giants. Lines 3-4: cf. Voluspo, 6.

Neither the Regius nor the Arnamagnæan Codex indicates a lacuna. Most editors have filled out the stanza with two lines from late paper manuscripts: "And both of these  shall ever be, / Till the gods to destruction go." Bugge ingeniously paraphrases Snorri's prose: "Vindsval's father  was Vosuth called, / And rough is all his race." Vindsval: "the Wind-Cold," also called Vindljoni, "the Wind-Man." Svosuth: "the Gentle."
Ymir's kin: the giants.

Bergelmir: when the gods slew Ymir in order to make the world out of his body, so much blood flowed from him that all the frost-giants were drowned except Bergelmir and his wife, who escaped in a boat; cf. stanza 35. Of Thruthgelmir ("the Mightily Burning") we know nothing, but Aurgelmir was the frost-giants' name for Ymir himself. Thus Ymir was the first of the giants, and so Othin's question is answered.

Snorri quotes this stanza, and the last two lines are taken from his version, as both of the manuscripts omit them. Elivagar ("Stormy Waves"): Mogk suggests that this river may have been the Milky Way. At any rate, the venom carried in its waters froze into ice-banks over Ginnunga-gap (the "yawning gap" referred to in Voluspo, 3), and then dripped down to make the giant Ymir.

Snorri gives, without materially elaborating on it, the same account of how Ymir's son and daughter were born under his left arm, and how his feet together created a son. That this offspring should have had six heads is nothing out of the ordinary, for various giants had more than the normal number, and Hymir's mother is credited with a little matter of nine hundred heads; cf. Hymiskvitha, 8. Of the career of Ymir's six-headed son we know nothing; he may have been the Thruthgelmir of stanza 29.
Snorri quotes this stanza. Bergelmir: on him and his boat cf. stanza 29 and note.
Snorri quotes this stanza. Hræsvelg ("the Corpse-Eater"): on this giant in eagle's form cf. Voluspo, 50, and Skirnismol, 27.

With this stanza the question-formula changes, and Othin's questions from this point on concern more or less directly the great final struggle. Line 4 is presumably spurious. Njorth: on Njorth and the Wanes, who gave him as a hostage to the gods at the end of their war, cf. Voluspo, 21 and note.

In both manuscripts, apparently through the carelessness of some older copyist, stanzas 40 and 41 are run together: "Eleventh answer me well, what men in the home mightily battle each day? They fell each other, and fare from the fight all healed full soon to sit." Luckily Snorri quotes stanza 41 in full, and the translation is from his version. Stanza 40 should probably run something like this: "Eleventh answer me well,  if thou knowest all / The fate that is fixed for the gods: / What men are they  who in Othin's home / Each day to fight go forth?"
The heroes: those brought to Valhall by the Valkyries. After the day's fighting they are healed of their wounds and all feast together.
Nine worlds: cf. Voluspo, 2. Niflhel: "Dark-Hell."
The mighty winter: Before the final destruction three winters follow one another with no intervening summers.

Snorri quotes this stanza. Hoddmimir's wood: probably this is the ash-tree Yggdrasil, which is sometimes referred to as "Mimir's Tree," because Mimir waters it from his well; cf. Voluspo, 27 and note, and Svipdagsmol, 30 and note. Hoddmimir is presumably another name for Mimir. Lif ("Life") and Lifthrasir ("Sturdy of Life"?): nothing further is known of this pair, from whom the new race of men is to spring.
Fenrir: there appears to be a confusion between the wolf Fenrir (cf. Voluspo, 39 and note) and his son, the wolf Skoll, who steals the sun (cf. Voluspo, 40 and note).
Snorri quotes this stanza. Alfrothul ("the Elf-Beam"): the sun.
Mogthrasir ("Desiring Sons"): not mentioned elsewhere in the Eddic poems, or by Snorri. The maidens: apparently Norns, like the "giant-maids" in Voluspo, 8. These Norns, however, are kindly to men.
Surt: cf. Voluspo, 52 and note.

Vithar: a son of Othin, who slays the wolf Fenrir; cf. Voluspo, 54 and note. Vali: the son whom Othin begot to avenge Baldr's death; cf. Voluspo, 33 and note. Mothi ("Wrath") and Magni ("Might"): the sons of the god Thor, who after his death inherit his famous hammer, Mjollnir. Concerning this hammer cf. especially Thrymskvitha, passim. Vingnir ("the Hurler"): Thor. Concerning his death cf. Voluspo, 56. This stanza is quoted by Snorri.
The wolf: Fenrir; cf. Voluspo, 53 and 54.

His son: Baldr. Bugge changes lines 3-4 to run: "What did Othin speak  in the ear of Baldr, / When to the bale-fire they bore him?" For Baldr's death cf. Voluspo, 32 and note. The question is, of course, unanswerable save by Othin himself, and so the giant at last recognizes his guest.
Fated: in stanza 19 Vafthruthnir was rash enough to wager his head against his guest's on the outcome of the contest of wisdom, so he knows that his defeat means his death.

intro_en: The Vafthruthnismol follows the Hovamol in the Codex Regius. From stanza 20 on it is also included in the Arnamagnæan Codex, the first part evidently having appeared on a leaf now lost. Snorri quotes eight stanzas of it in the Prose Edda, and in his prose text closely paraphrases many others.

The poem is wholly in dialogue form except for a single narrative stanza (stanza 5). After a brief introductory discussion between Othin and his wife, Frigg, concerning the reputed wisdom of the giant Vafthruthnir, Othin, always in quest of wisdom, seeks out the giant, calling himself Gagnrath. The giant immediately insists that they shall demonstrate which is the wiser of the two, and propounds four questions (stanzas 11, 13, 15, and 17), each of which Othin answers. It is then the god's turn to ask, and he begins with a series of twelve numbered questions regarding the origins and past history of life. These Vafthruthnir answers, and Othin asks five more questions, this time referring to what is to follow the destruction of the gods, the last one asking the name of his own slayer. Again Vafthruthnir answers, and Othin finally propounds the unanswerable question: "What spake Othin himself in the ears of his son, ere in the bale-fire he burned?" Vafthruthnir, recognizing his questioner as Othin himself, admits his inferiority in wisdom, and so the contest ends.

The whole poem is essentially encyclopædic in character, and thus was particularly useful to Snorri in his preparation of the Prose Edda. The encyclopædic poem with a slight narrative outline seems to have been exceedingly popular; the Grimnismol and the much later Alvissmol represent different phases of the same type. The Vafthruthnismol and Grimnismol together, indeed, constitute a fairly complete dictionary of Norse mythology. There has been much discussion as to the probable date of the Vafthruthnismol, but it appears to belong to about the same period as the Voluspo: in other words, the middle of the tenth century. While there may be a few interpolated passages in the poem as we now have it, it is clearly a united whole, and evidently in relatively good condition.
